newsitem.title: USA: Calif. lawmakers propose zero-based budgeting.
newsitem.headline: Calif. lawmakers propose zero-based budgeting.

text.p: A bipartisan team of California lawmakers has reintroduced a proposal to overhaul the state's annual budgeting process, their offices said on Tuesday.
Last year, the state Assembly and Senate approved a similar measure, but it was vetoed by Gov. Pete Wilson.

This time, Democrat State Sen. Jack O'Connell and Republican Sen. Tim Leslie introduced their zero-based budgeting proposal as a bill that would require Wilson's support and as a constitutional amendment that would bypass Wilson and appear on the state ballot for voter approval.

California's Constitution requires the governor each year to submit to the state legislature a budget itemizing state expenditures and estimating state revenues, and requires the legislature to pass the budget bill by midnight on June 15.
The twin measures introduced by O'Connell and Leslie would require so-called zero-based budgeting in putting together the annual blueprint for state spending.
Zero-based budgeting is a process that requires state agencies to start with a base of zero dollars, adding funding for programs deemed appropriate.
If approved, the proposed budgeting reforms would take effect July 1, 1999.
Some lawmakers contend the reforms would lead to greater fiscal responsibility and would make it easier to review the governor's annual spending proposals.
Wilson's Department of Finance said a similar attempt at zero-based budgeting in the 1970s was a failure, was time-consuming and costly, and did not affect budget decisions.
H.D. Palmer, a spokesman for the Department of Finance, said the Wilson administration would oppose the proposal.
"We think we have a better way of getting to the same goal," Palmer said.
